title: Working Interests
metaTitle: Selling a Working Interest in West Virginia Oil & Gas
metaDescription: Hold a working interest with West Virginia drilling and operating cost exposure? We confirm the operating agreement and joint interest billing before buying.
heroLead: A working interest is the one mineral asset in West Virginia where you're on the hook for costs as well as entitled to revenue, and that changes the whole conversation compared to a royalty.
intro: A working interest gives the holder the right to explore for and produce oil and gas, but also carries a proportionate share of the costs of drilling, completing and operating the well, unlike a royalty interest, which is free of those costs. In West Virginia, working interests most often show up with small legacy owners, individuals or families who participated financially in an older vertical well, sometimes decades ago, in the Big Injun, Gordon or another shallow sand, and still hold a fractional working interest subject to ongoing joint interest billing from the operator.
Because a working interest comes with both upside and cost exposure, valuing one requires looking at the operating agreement and recent billing history, not merely a royalty check.

sections.heading: Why working interests carry cost exposure a royalty doesn't
paragraphs: A working interest owner is billed their proportionate share of operating expenses, workovers, and any capital costs the operator incurs on the well or unit, deducted against their share of production revenue rather than paid separately. On an older, marginal well past its productive peak, operating costs can approach or even exceed revenue in a slow month, meaning a small working interest can occasionally generate a net bill rather than a net payment. This is the central risk that distinguishes a working interest from every other mineral interest type, and it's the first thing we evaluate.
We ask for recent joint interest billing statements alongside any revenue statements to see the real net picture before valuing your interest.

sections.heading: Reading the operating agreement itself
paragraphs: The joint operating agreement governing your well specifies how costs are allocated, what happens if a working interest owner doesn't pay their share, and whether there are any preferential rights or consent requirements attached to a transfer of the interest. Some older West Virginia operating agreements include a right of first refusal for other working interest owners in the unit, which can affect how a sale needs to be structured and who needs to be notified before closing.
We review this agreement specifically, since working interest transfers sometimes require more coordination with the operator or other owners than a straightforward mineral or royalty sale would.

sections.heading: Legacy vertical well working interests versus modern horizontal units
paragraphs: Most working interests we see in West Virginia trace back to small, local participation in shallow vertical wells drilled before the horizontal shale era, often a modest cash investment made by a family decades ago in exchange for a small percentage working interest. These wells are typically well past peak production now, which means the cost-versus-revenue balance matters more than it would have in the well's early years. We look at recent production and cost trends for the specific well, not general county activity, since working interest value is tied tightly to that individual well's current economics.

sections.heading: What we need to evaluate a working interest
paragraphs: We want the joint operating agreement, your assignment or participation document establishing the interest, and at least six months of joint interest billing and revenue statements. That billing history is the single most useful document for a working interest, since it shows the actual net economics rather than a gross revenue figure that doesn't account for your cost exposure.

faqs.question: What's the difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.answer: A working interest carries a proportionate share of drilling and operating costs along with production revenue. A royalty interest receives revenue free of those costs. Working interests carry more risk and require more paperwork to evaluate.

faqs.question: Can a working interest actually lose money in a given month?
faqs.answer: Yes, particularly on an older, marginal well where operating costs and any workover expenses can approach or exceed that month's revenue share. This is why we review joint interest billing history rather than valuing off a single payment.

faqs.question: Do I need the other working interest owners' permission to sell mine?
faqs.answer: Sometimes. Some joint operating agreements include a right of first refusal for other owners in the unit. We check your specific agreement to confirm what's required before closing.

faqs.question: My working interest comes from an old vertical well my grandfather invested in. Is it still worth anything?
faqs.answer: Possibly, depending on the well's current production and cost trend. Many legacy shallow wells are past peak production, so we look closely at recent billing and revenue statements to determine real current value.

faqs.question: What documents speed up a working interest sale?
faqs.answer: The joint operating agreement, the assignment or participation document establishing your interest, and at least six months of joint interest billing statements are the most useful starting point.

faqs.question: Does selling a working interest transfer my cost exposure to the buyer?
faqs.answer: Yes. Once the sale closes and the assignment is recorded, future drilling and operating costs, along with future revenue, become the buyer's responsibility, not yours, going forward.
